Unlike forward mapping, it avoids gaps and overlaps inherent in geometry deformation, ensuring every pixel is covered by a valid texture lookup [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the rendering technique uses 'backward mapping' to 'distort the associated texture coordinates' instead of deforming the geometry. It further explains that this approach allows 'planar and view-aligned slices to be rendered with modified 3D texture coordinates.' In computer graphics, backward mapping (calculating source texture coordinates for each destination pixel) is the standard method to ensure that every pixel in the output image is covered by a valid texture lookup, thereby avoiding the gaps and overlaps (holes) that are inherent in forward mapping (projecting source pixels to destination space) when dealing with complex deformations. The evidence supports the claim that this method avoids the issues associated with geometry deformation by using texture coordinate distortion.
